overview: The National Belle—also documented as the National Bell—was one of the defining mines of the Red Mountain district and a major anchor for Red Mountain Town.

Society of Economic Geologists research records that the mine became famous in 1883 when miners encountered the first of several ore-lined caverns or “great pockets.” The mineralized pockets included silver- and copper-bearing sulfides and sulfosalts with lead-zinc minerals and quartz-barite gangue, helping drive investment and settlement around the mine.

timeline.text: Sources: Society of Economic Geologists Guidebook 3, “Great Pockets: the National Belle mine” (1988); Fort Lewis College Red Mountain Project.

moreHistory: Fort Lewis College’s Red Mountain Project confirms that the developing town shifted toward the National Belle as the toll-road and Silverton Railroad corridor took shape.
Surviving identification features include the shaft/headframe area, dumps, structural remnants, and the adjoining but distinct Red Mountain townsite and railroad landscape.

Component safeguard: keep the National Belle mine/shaft, Red Mountain Town, Silverton Railroad facilities, nearby Yankee Girl/Guston/Genesee workings, and later district consolidation as separate linked records.
